subject: Cognitive Science
title: Decision Hygiene
description: A short lesson to help you apply Decision Hygiene.

hook.text: Two judges sentence differently for the same crime depending on whether it's before or after lunch.

buildup.text: Kahneman's "decision hygiene" applies noise reduction to judgment: structure processes to cut variability.

discovery.text: Noise is random error: different judges, different days, different moods produce different decisions on the same case.

twist.text: Noise is as damaging as bias but gets far less attention. We fix bias and ignore the randomness.

climax.text: Structured interviews, checklists, and independent evaluations are proven noise-reducers that anyone can use.

punchline.text: Good process matters more than good intentions.

quiz.question: What is noise in decision-making?
options: Random variability in judgments on the same case

details.summary: Decision hygiene, a framework from Daniel Kahneman, refers to systematic procedures that reduce noise and bias in collective judgments without requiring deep understanding of specific biases. It includes independent evaluation, structured assessment, and aggregation of diverse judgments.
details.whyItMatters: Decision hygiene is more practical than trying to eliminate individual biases. Organizations that adopt noise-reducing procedures make consistently better decisions across hiring, medicine, and law.
takeaways: Decision hygiene reduces noise and bias through procedure
Independent evaluation before group discussion prevents anchoring
Structured processes outperform unstructured expert judgment

faq.question: What is the difference between noise and bias in decisions?
faq.answer: Bias is a systematic error in one direction. Noise is unwanted variability in judgments that should be consistent. Two judges sentencing the same case differently is noise. Both degrade decision quality, but noise is often overlooked while bias gets all the attention.

faq.question: What are the key principles of decision hygiene?
faq.answer: Have each evaluator form an independent judgment before group discussion. Use structured criteria rather than holistic impressions. Break complex judgments into components. Aggregate multiple independent assessments. These steps reduce both noise and the influence of individual biases.
